label: text
text: - The Chinese who was acting as assistant cashier of the Wing On Bank at the time of the incidents in regard to which two men are charged with conspiracy to defraud the Bank, admitted under cross-examination by Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn that he had made a false answer at the Magistracy.

label: text
text: There was a sensation in court as this morning's hearing of the charge of conspiring to defraud the Wing On Bank was drawing to its conclusion.

label: text
text: The statement concerned a question by Mr. Zeitlyn at the Magistracy as to whether witness (the assistant cashier) had ever paid out large sums on forged documents before the events with which this particular case was concerned.

label: text
text: At the Magistracy, witness had denied that he had ever done so but this morning, in reply to Mr. Zeildlyn, he said that this answer was false and that the truth was that he had paid out two large sums on forged documents shortly before this particular ense, both of which were in the neighbourhood of $20,000 to $30,000.

label: text
text: Witness's explanation of the false reply was that the matter was a company secret and that he had been warned that he must not divulge it.

label: text
text:
Witness's Hesitation:
Asked who had so instructed him, witness replied after considerable hesitancy that the chief manager had:

label: text
text: Witness was reminded by Mr. Zeitlys that he had been on his oath to tell the truth at the Magistracy as he was now.

label: text
text: Witness replied that he was an employee of the company and he considered it his duty not to tell when he had been so instructed.

label: text
text:
Asked who would be personally responsible for the money which was lost to the company by the forgeries, witness replied that he himself was and the chief cashier.
— Mr. Zeitlyn: And the fact that you were responsible for these large sums of money would make a big impression on you, wouldn't it?

label: text
text:
Witness: I knew that I was re-
sponsible.

label: text
text: Mr. Zeitlyn: Were you to pay back the $50,000 involved in this case, as well as the sums 'on' the other, forged documents?

label: text
text: Witness: I was reprimanded about being careful but nothing else was said about the $50,000 involved in this case.

label: text
text: Mr. Zeitlyn: You are absolutely certain about this?

label: text
text: Mr. Zeitlyn: And always have been?

label: text
text: Witness: Yes.

label: text
text: Mr. Zeitlyn: Then how do you account for the note of the magistrate at the police court which records that in the answers you gave me there you said that you could not remember what Mr. Phillip Gock-chin, the Chief Manager, said about this matter, whether he was angry or whether "we should be held responsible." The Magistrate's note records that you replied to my question on this matter after a period of hesitation and that you said you could not remember whether you were told that you might have to make good the amount.

label: text
text: Witness: I remember now that nothing was said about my being held responsible.

label: paragraph_title
text: BLAZE AT WELLINGTON

label: text
text: A MORNING CALL

label: text
text: The third floor of No. 162, Wellington Street, used as an enting house, was gutted in a fire which broke out on this part of the building this morning. The flames had secured a good hold when the alarm was received at the Central Fire Station, but the efforts of the fire-fighters to quell the outbreak proved successful after considerable labour.

label: text
text: The inmates of all the floors look to the street on the alarm being given and there were no asualties.

label: text
text: Besides the third floor, which was left with the bare walls standing, the flames worked into a part of the second floor used as a restaurant. The contents of the floors below were damaged by water.

label: text
text: The extent of the damage has not been assessed: It is understood that the building was insured for $4,000.

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: TWO MOTOR CASES AND A DEATH.

label: text
text:
Driving a motor car at Coronation Road yesterday afternoon, Mrs. Geldart, of Torres Building, Kowloon, ran into a Chinese girl who came from the rear of a bus.
The girl received injuries to the face and was taken by Mr. Geldart in her car to the Kowloon Hospital and later to the Kwong Wah Hospital. On inquiries being made by the police after a report was made, it was found that the girl had been removed by her people after receiving attention.

label: text
text: At 2.30 this morning a motor bus ran into two ricsha coolies at Gascoigne Road, necessitating the removal of the men to the Kwong Wah Hospital. The driver of the bus has been detained.

label: text
text: While sitting over the edge of a Taikoo Sugar Refinery lighter lying alongside the wharf at North Point, a member of the crew dropped into the water at 7 o'clock this morning.

label: text
text: The coxswain heard the call "man overboard" and promptly threw a rope. An attempt was made by the unfortunate man to reach the rope, but failing in this he was carried away by the strong current flowing at the time and lost.

label: paragraph_title
text: PROTEST "STRIKE."

label: text
text: HOIHOW MERCHANTS AGAINST PICKETS

label: text
text: BOYCOTT BOYCOTTED

label: text
text: A boycott has been declared by the merchants of Hoihow against the pickets, who are maintaining the anti-foreign boycott at that port.

label: text
text: As a matter of fact, the commercial interests have suspended operations against what they consider to be the high-handed action of the local boycott committee.

label: text
text: This Monday, a foreign steamer (said to be the "Mingsang") was in port. A junk, loaded with poultry for export, was making for the ship when pickets—vigil

label: text
text: ance having been increased on the steamer's arrival—gave chase. Rather than let the goods fall into the hands of the pickets, the shippers' fokis threw most of it overboard. As the birds were in baskets in crates, some of the

label: text
text: abandoned poultry was retrieved. At any rate, one foki was arrested. He was sentenced by a "committee of cargo, investigation-tion" to be marched, in shame, around the town, as a lesson to others.

label: text
text: The mercantile bodies considered the punishment too harsh. Business organisations decided that doors should be closed in protest.

label: text
text: Several hundred men are also reported to have marched to local government offices to petition redress.

label: text
text: A subsequent incident was the capture of one of several lecturers (or street speakers) sent out by semi-official authorities. He fell into the hands of a crowd but was rescued by the action of boycott pickets, who took into custody a bad character.

label: text
text: A peculiar accident occurred at Bonham Road yesterday as Dr. W. B. A. Moore, of the Victoria Hospital, was riding in a ricsha. One wheel of the vehicle dropped out and the coolie was knocked down to the ground by receiving a prod on his side with a portion of the shaft.

label: text
text: Dr. Moore was not hurt and escaped with a mere shaking. The coolie was struck in the region of his spleen and also received abrasions to the right ankle.

label: paragraph_title
text: SILVER DRUMS

label: text
text: UNIQUE PRESENTATION TO SURREYS

label: paragraph_title
text: TRIPPEC CEREMONY.

label: text
text:
A unique occasion in that it was a triple ceremony was observed today by the 1st Battalion, the East Surrey Regiment, which assembled about 700 strong on the Murray parade ground this morning.
It was a parade typical of the solemn pageantry of the British Army. Those who could get away from business and a number of ladies gathered in the stand, and were duly impressed.

label: text
text: First, H.E. the Governor (Sir Cecil Clementi) arrived, with Lady Clementi, and was accorded a Royal salute.

label: text
text: H.E. the General Officer Commanding, Major-General C.C. Lund, then came on the ground, accompanied by his A.D.C., and inspected the battallion.

label: text
text: The old drums were trooped off, passing through the whole of the lines (drawn up on three sides of a square).

label: text
text: The Rev. G. F. Stopford, C.F., pronounced the blessing on the silver drums, which were placed on a stand in front of the saluting base.

label: text
text: Lt.-Col. F. S. Montague Bates, who commands the battalion; then addressed his men.

label: text
text: reys were stationed at Agra when an epidemic carried off five officers and a number of men, including 2nd Lieut. Walker, Mrs. Walker, mother of Lt. Walker, had since died and bequeathed $1,000 to the regiment for a memorial for her son. With this sum, the set of silver drums had been purchased and would be used by the battalion on ceremonial occasions. They would be kept in the officers' mess at Murray Barracks.

label: text
text: To-day was also the anniversary of the second battle of Ypres, in which the East Surrey Regiment took part. The Colonel recalled the part taken by both battalions. Fifteen officers (including Major R. W. Paterson) were lost in addition to 264 other ranks. The 1st Battalion behaved with great gallantry in the defence of Hill 60, and won three V.C.'s and many other decorations.

label: text
text: Mrs. Luard then made the official presentation of the drums, each drummer stepping forward in turn.

label: text
text:
G.O.C.'s Congratulations.
Major-General Luard congratulated the battalion on its splendid turn-out and its achievement, referring to it as one of the best he had seen.

label: text
text: The triple part of the ceremony came in the decoration, by the G.O.C., of Sergeant Drummer French, with the long service and good conduct medal (minimum of 18 years' service). His Excellency congratulated the recipient and pointed to him as an example to the many young soldiers on parade.

label: text
text: Subsequently, the Surreys marched past, played by their band and drummers. At the saluting base, at which the Union Jack had been broken, were the Governor, the General and their ladies.

label: text
text: Among the spectators were noticed Commodore A. J. Stirling R.N., and Major Macready, D.A.A. Q.M.G.

label: text
text: It being St. George's Day, the soldiers wore the red and white roses in their helmets. The Sergeant Drummer, in his attractive uniform, had the flowers in his helmet, on his drumstick and on his chest.

label: text
text: This afternoon, two football matches will be played, it being a holiday.

label: text
text: The Privates, who supply most of the Battalion first eleven, are to play the Corporals; and the officers meet the sergeants.
